title: Mastering the Miosis: Cataract Surgery in the Small Pupil
summary: Managing a small pupil (<5mm) is a critical skill for the cataract surgeon. This guide explores the etiology, pharmacological strategies, and mechanical expansion techniques required to ensure safe phacoemulsification and minimize intraoperative complications like iris trauma or posterior capsule rupture.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: In cataract surgery, a 'small pupil' is generally defined as a pupil diameter of less than 5mm that fails to dilate adequately with standard preoperative mydriatics. Inadequate visualization increases the risk of iris damage, incomplete capsulorhexis, and posterior capsule rupture (PCR). Optimal visualization requires at least a 5.0 to 5.5mm aperture for safe phacoemulsification.

sections.title: Etiology: Why is the Pupil Small?
Intraoperative Floppy Iris Syndrome (IFIS)
content: Classic Triad: Billowing flaccid iris, progressive intraoperative miosis, and iris prolapse toward incisions.
Primary Trigger: Tamsulosin (Flomax) and other alpha-1 antagonists.
Risk: Can occur even years after discontinuing the medication.
Management: Requires specialized techniques; epinephrine in bag, Healon5, or rings.

sections.title: Preoperative Assessment & Workup
content: Detailed Drug History: Specific focus on BPH medications (Tamsulosin, Silodosin).
Slit-Lamp Exam: Check for PXF material on lens capsule or pupillary margin.
Gonioscopy: Assess for peripheral anterior synechiae (PAS).
Dilation Testing: Measure maximum dilation with Phenylephrine 10% and Tropicamide 1%.
Corneal Endothelium: Assess health, as small pupil surgery increases surgical time and endothelial stress.

rows: Maintains dilation and prevents miosis during surgery.
Useful in rigid pupils or pediatric cases.
Can provide mild mydriasis and patient comfort.

content.explanation: Epinephrine (0.1% bisulfite-free), Lidocaine (1% preservative-free), and Shugarcaine (the mixture). Mix 3cc Lidocaine + 9cc BSS + 0.25cc Epinephrine. Effectively dilates and stabilizes the iris.

sections.title: Mechanical Expansion: Step-by-Step
content: Step 1: Synechiolysis using a cyclodialysis spatula or iris sweep.
Step 2: Viscomydriasis using Healon5 or cohesive OVD to push iris margins.
Step 3: Pupillary Stretching (e.g., Beehler or 2-instrument stretch).
Step 4: Pupillary Expansion Device insertion (Malyugin Ring or Iris Hooks).
Step 5: Completion of capsulorhexis and phacoemulsification.
Step 6: Device removal and Miochol injection for miosis.

rows: Single incision, easy to use, square-shaped pupil.
Cost, risk of catching the capsule during removal.
Can cause sphincter tears and bleeding.

sections.title: Surgical Pearls for Success
content: Lower Phaco Parameters: Reduce flow and vacuum to minimize iris 'chatter' and attraction to the tip.
Bimanual Manipulation: Use a second instrument to tuck iris away or stabilize the nucleus.
Capsulorhexis Size: Aim for 5.0 - 5.5mm. Use the ring or hooks as a template for size.
Cortical Cleanup: Use 'tangential' stripping to remove cortex hidden under the iris/ring.
OVD Management: Use cohesive OVD to maintain space and dispersive OVD to protect the endothelium.

sections.title: Intraoperative Red Flags
content: Iris Prolapse: Usually indicates high posterior pressure or IFIS. Do not just push it back; reduce inflow and use cohesive OVD.
Sphincter Tears: Avoid aggressive stretching in fibrotic pupils (PXF/Uveitis).
Shadowing/Poor View: Never proceed with phaco if the capsulorhexis edge isn't visible.
Zonular Dialysis: Small pupils are highly correlated with PXF and weak zonules.

sections.title: Landmark Studies
sections.content: Chang & Campbell (2005) first described IFIS and its association with Tamsulosin. The study emphasized that even short-term use of alpha-blockers could lead to permanent iris structural changes. The Malyugin Ring study (2007) demonstrated that mechanical expansion significantly reduced PCR rates in small pupil cases compared to manual stretching.
